extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of English Renaissance poetry; readers of Sidney and poetic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing or producing Elizabethan/Renaissance poetry (sonnets, songs, pastorals) with reference to Sidneyan poetics: the poet's aims, style, and moral/social functions. Includes guidance on poetic thought, diction, originality, and the poet’s superiority to other arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style of prose: plain, manly English without Euphuism
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe the playfulness in Sidney’s opening and close of a treatise written throughout in plain, manly English without Euphuism, and strictly reasoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial preference for clear, vigorous diction and logical argument over ornate, affected manner (Euphuism). The comment is applied to Sidney’s treatise style and implies a standard for critical prose and poetic defence: favour plainness and strict reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry the first Light-giver
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a principle/headline: poetry’s role is to illuminate (give 'light') — an evaluative standard that poetry should enlighten, instruct, or reveal truths to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry is the one creative art (not mere reportage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is the one creative art. Astronomers and others repeat what they find.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes poetry from sciences or descriptive arts: poets create or imaginatively shape material rather than merely reporting facts. When evaluating poetry, value imaginative creation and generative treatment of subject matter rather than simple factual repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets improve Nature
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sidneyan claim that poets do not merely copy nature but rectify/augment it — the poet should idealize, refine or 'improve' natural types. A poem’s success can be judged by how well it elevates or perfects its material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets idealize man
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry's task includes creating idealized representations of human character and action. Evaluation should attend to how poetry universalizes or exemplifies human qualities in an elevated, exemplary fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essence of poetry is in thought, not ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Its essence is in the thought, not in apparelling of verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority for substantive intellectual/contentual qualities (idea, moral, imaginative truth) over merely decorative verbal ornament. Judges should privilege clarity and force of thought above rhetorical surface or metrical dress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry advances virtuous action — moral usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry best advances the end of all earthly learning, virtuous action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims a pragmatic/moral function for poetry: it should promote virtue and ethical ends. When assessing poetry, consider whether and how it fosters virtuous behavior or moral insight (an advantage claimed over mere philosophy or history).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry’s advantage over Moral Philosophy and History
rubrics_metrics.description: Its advantage herein over Moral Philosophy. Its advantage herein over History.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sidney argues poetry has specific advantages: it can motivate virtue more effectively than moral philosophy and convey general truths better than history. Evaluation should consider poetry’s capacity to move readers morally and to present general/typical truths rather than only particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry conveys general truth; History records particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not by writing in verse or prose that the Historian and Poet are distinguished. The one relates what has been, the other what might be. Poetry is chiefly conversant about general truth; History about particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this Aristotelian distinction to judge poems: good poetry represents universal human behaviours/likelihoods (what might or ought to be), rather than merely chronicling particular events. Evaluate for generality, exemplarity, and psychological plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet surpasses the Philosopher in certain aims
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet’s Work and Parts... In what manner the Poet goes beyond Philosopher, Historian, and all others (bating comparison with the Divine). He is beyond the Philosopher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sidneyan claim that poets can achieve what philosophers cannot (particularly in moving the will and imagination). Evaluate poetic effectiveness relative to philosophical abstraction: does the poem achieve imaginative moral persuasion or insight that philosophy alone cannot?

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mediocrity; high standard for poets
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace’s “Ars Poetica”... 'Neither men, gods, nor lettered columns have admitted mediocrity in poets.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit injunction that poets must strive for excellence; mediocrity is not acceptable. Judges/editors should apply rigorous standards and not tolerate half-hearted or bland verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hackneyed common-places and overused quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent resort to the Polyanthea caused many a good quotation to be hackneyed; the term of rhetoric, 'a common-place,' came then to mean a good saying made familiar by incessant quoting... any trite saying good or bad, but commonly without wit in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautionary point about reliance on stock commonplaces: originality of thought and freshness of expression are valued. When evaluating, penalize clichés and overused rhetorical tropes; reward inventive phrasing and authentic insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Poet’s Work: what poetry does for us
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet’s Work and Parts. § 1. WORK: What Poetry does for us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing rubric: consider the functional roles of poetry (moral instruction, delight, imitation of life, etc.) when evaluating. This is an overarching standard to measure poems against their social/intellectual effects.
